title: Algorithm Design
summary: Half the grade is a three-hour programming exam on WebLab with five or six Java tasks, one or two per paradigm, graded by hand on correctness and efficiency. The other half is written: a 90-minute midterm on greedy and divide and conquer and a 90-minute endterm on dynamic programming and network flow, or one three-hour resit on everything. The written papers are open questions only: proofs, hand traces, recurrences and network models.

basis.note: The three latest sittings, each a written and a digital paper; the archive holds 17 more (2020 to 2025). Shares are point shares per paper, weighted by the paper's weight in the final grade: each digital paper and written resit 0.5, the written endterm 0.3 (it is 0.6 of W). Topic of a digital task text given only on paper is read from its solution code.

format.mode: Written: closed-book open questions on paper. Digital: Java programming in WebLab (IntelliJ available), closed book apart from the Java 17 API docs
format.duration: Written midterm and endterm 90 minutes each, written resit 3 hours, digital exam 3 hours
format.structure: Written midterm and endterm: six or seven open questions of 20 to 27 points, one module pair each. Written resit: 11 or 12 questions of 40 points over all four modules. Digital: five or six tasks worth 10 points, ordered greedy, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, network flow, each with public tests; the final mark comes from hand grading.
format.grading: W = 0.4 W1 + 0.6 W2; final grade 0.5 W + 0.5 P, but if W or P is below 5 the final grade is the lower of the two. A resit of W is one three-hour exam on everything; W and P can be resat separately. Partial results last one academic year. Written points convert as 1 + 9 times the score share.
format.aids: None on the written papers: no book, notes or calculator. In the digital exam only the Java API documentation and the network flow library supplied in WebLab.

topicWeights.asks: Write OPT with base cases and initial call for a new story problem, extend a known recurrence with an extra parameter, fill a weighted interval or edge-selection table and trace back the choice, state time and minimal space, and implement an iterative solution or rebuild one from a given table.

Build a network for an assignment problem with minimum and maximum limits, remove lower bounds step by step, prove that a min cut gives the optimum of a two-way split, adapt baseball elimination or a matching model, and code a model with the library.

topicWeights.topic: Greedy scheduling, caching and Huffman codes
topicWeights.asks: A counterexample to a wrong greedy rule, then a 5-point exchange or stays-ahead proof for the right one, a farthest-in-future trace, and programming tasks on interval partitioning, Huffman-style merging or scheduling by sort order.

Solve a recurrence with the master method in three marked steps, design a recursive algorithm for a new problem (majority element, L-shaped tiling), count multiplications in fast exponentiation, and code maximum subarray or counting inversions recursively.

Find a minimum cut and its capacity from a given flow, run scaling Ford-Fulkerson phase by phase, change a capacity to create an augmenting path, give the running time of build plus max flow, and counterexamples on unique cuts and flows.

topicWeights.topic: Minimum spanning trees, shortest paths and clustering
topicWeights.asks: Apply the cut or cycle property to a graph and state the MST consequence, and in the programming exam a maximum-spacing clustering with Kruskal and union-find.

questionTypes.description: Digital tasks: implement the most efficient algorithm in Java for a story problem, often a variant of a course problem, with the network flow library for flow tasks.
Solve a recurrence, fill a DP table, run scaling Ford-Fulkerson, read a min cut off a flow, build a given network for an instance or trace a greedy rule.
On paper: write a recurrence with its call, a divide and conquer procedure, a loop order, or a change to a network model, with a short explanation.
Exchange-argument and greedy-stays-ahead proofs, and proofs that a cut capacity equals the objective of a flow model.
Give a small instance showing that a greedy rule, an unmodified recurrence or a claim about cuts and flows fails.
State and justify the time or the minimal space of a DP or a flow-based algorithm.

recurring: Both analysed written resits have a 3-point master-method recurrence, marked in three steps (leaves, case, answer); the coverage tables on the papers list one on the recent midterms too.
A greedy problem in two steps: disprove a suggested rule with an instance, then prove the correct rule with a 5-point exchange or stays-ahead argument.
A 3-point DP table question on the 2025 endterm and resit: complete a partly given OPT, fill the table from index 0 and trace back the chosen intervals or edges.
A known recurrence (weighted interval scheduling, subset sum, the restaurant shifts) is extended with an extra constraint, and you must update the call too.
A two-way split solved by a min cut (two people sharing tasks, lectures versus tutorials), with a proof that the cut capacity is the cost.
An assignment network with lower bounds that you must turn into a circulation, on paper and in code.
Each digital exam has one or two tasks per paradigm in a fixed order (greedy, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, network flow), and the DP and flow tasks together carry 5 or 6 of the 10 points.
trends: Up to 2022-23 the written papers had a multiple-choice part worth 30 percent and the digital exam came in two parts; since 2023-24 the written papers are open questions only and the digital exam is one three-hour sitting.
The 2022-23 papers weighted the digital exams at 60 percent of the final grade; the current rule is 50 percent each.
Questions now reuse earlier problems: the 2025 resit continues the poem problem of the 2025 endterm, and resit digital tasks extend endterm tasks such as the judo camp.
strategy: Prepare for the two halves separately: a strong written grade cannot rescue a programming grade below 5, or the other way round.
Memorise the proof templates for greedy (both styles) and the cut-capacity proof for min-cut models; they return almost word for word with new problems.
For every OPT you write, check that the base cases fit the initial call and that no maximum can return plus infinity.
In the programming exam, first get a correct solution, then make it asymptotically optimal; a slower one loses points, and partial steps still earn credit.
Do not trust the spec tests: grading is manual, and a boolean task can pass many tests by always returning the same value.
Practise coding network models with the supplied Graph, Node and Edge library, including demands and lower bounds, before the exam.
On the 20-point 2025 endterm you have 4.5 minutes per point; do the trace and recurrence questions first and leave the proofs for after.
pitfalls: Turning a lower-bound problem into a circulation by adding only an infinite edge from t to s, which drops the rule that everyone must be assigned.
Answering a counterexample question about circulations with an all-zero flow, which the 2025 endterm marking notes call a very common mistake.
In exchange proofs, defining an inversion without the inequality between the jobs or deriving the contradiction from a wrong assumption.
Claiming that two cuts or two flows exist without writing them out: the 2024 resit gave at most 1 of 2 points for counterexamples without explicit cuts and flows.
In digital tasks, forgetting one cost or bound, such as the cleaning time in a schedule or one of the limits in a model: the reference code checks exactly those versions.
